questions.title: GC Algorithms Comparison
questions.question: What are the main GC algorithms in Java and how do you choose between them?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **G1GC (default Java 9+): low-pause, balanced throughput — good general choice**
- **ZGC/Shenandoah: ultra-low pause (< 10ms) — for latency-sensitive workloads**
- **ParallelGC: maximum throughput, high pauses — for batch processing**
- **GC pause = stop-the-world: all application threads halt**
- **Tune GC by measuring, not guessing — use GC logs**
- **Major GC pauses are the symptom; find the root cause (leak, undersized heap)**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Java has several GC algorithms with different trade-offs between throughput, pause time, and memory overhead.

G1GC is the default since Java 9 and a good general-purpose choice. It divides the heap into regions and collects the highest-garbage regions first, aiming to meet a pause time target. It works well for heaps from 4GB to 32GB.

ZGC and Shenandoah are designed for latency-sensitive workloads where even short pauses are unacceptable — they achieve sub-10ms pause times regardless of heap size by doing most GC work concurrently with the application. The trade-off is slightly lower throughput.

ParallelGC prioritizes throughput over pauses — it uses multiple threads for GC but still pauses the application. Good for batch processing where throughput matters more than individual request latency.

In practice, start with G1GC, enable GC logging, measure pause times, and only switch algorithms if measurements show pauses are actually a problem.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## GC Algorithm Comparison

```
Algorithm   | Default For  | Pause Time     | Throughput | Memory Overhead | Best For
------------|--------------|----------------|------------|-----------------|---------------------------
SerialGC    | Single-core  | High (seconds) | Low        | Low             | Embedded, micro services
ParallelGC  | Java 8       | Medium (100ms+)| High       | Low             | Batch processing, analytics
G1GC        | Java 9-21    | Low (< 200ms)  | Medium     | Medium          | General purpose, web apps
ZGC         | Java 15+     | Ultra-low(1ms) | Medium     | High            | Latency-critical (trading)
Shenandoah  | OpenJDK      | Ultra-low(1ms) | Medium     | High            | Same as ZGC
```

## Configuring GC

```bash
# G1GC (recommended for most Spring Boot apps)
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200 \\     # Target pause: G1 TRIES to stay under this
  -XX:G1HeapRegionSize=16m \\     # Region size (auto-tuned if not set)
  -XX:G1NewSizePercent=20 \\      # Min Young Gen as % of heap
  -XX:G1MaxNewSizePercent=40 \\   # Max Young Gen as % of heap
  -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time:filecount=5,filesize=10m \
  -jar myapp.jar

# ZGC (Java 15+, for < 10ms pause requirement)
java -Xms8g -Xmx8g \
  -XX:+UseZGC \
  -XX:ZCollectionInterval=1 \\   # Force GC at least every 1 second
  -jar myapp.jar
# ZGC is generational in Java 21+ (-XX:+ZGenerational)

# Parallel GC (batch jobs)
java -Xms4g -Xmx4g \
  -XX:+UseParallelGC \
  -XX:ParallelGCThreads=8 \\    # Use 8 threads for GC
  -jar batch-processor.jar
```

## GC Log Analysis

```
G1GC log output (with -Xlog:gc):

[0.245s] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause)
          Eden: 256M->0M, Survivors: 0->32M, Old: 0->12M
          Heap: 256M->44M
          3.123ms         ← Pause time

[5.234s] GC(14) Pause Young (Normal) 128M->45M(2048M) 4.5ms

[30.456s] GC(89) Pause Full (Allocation Failure)
           Heap: 1900M->800M(2048M) 1456ms  ← PROBLEM! 1.4 second pause

DIAGNOSIS:
  'Pause Full (Allocation Failure)' → Old Gen full → emergency Full GC
  Causes:
    1. Memory leak: objects accumulating in Old Gen
    2. Heap too small for workload
    3. Too many long-lived objects (caches, static state)

  Solutions:
    1. Take heap dump, analyze with Eclipse MAT or VisualVM
    2. Increase -Xmx (if leak isn't the cause)
    3. Review caching strategy (Caffeine with size limit instead of HashMap)
```

## Understanding GC Phases (G1GC)

```
G1GC PHASES:

1. Minor GC / Young GC (Concurrent):
   - Triggered when Eden fills
   - Stop-the-world: typically 5-50ms
   - Evacuates live objects from Eden → Survivors or Old Gen
   - Frequency: every few seconds under normal load

2. Concurrent Marking (runs WHILE app is running):
   - G1 tracks which objects are live
   - No pause — runs concurrently
   - Starts when heap occupancy > InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (default 45%)

3. Mixed GC:
   - After marking, G1 knows which Old Gen regions have most garbage
   - Collects Young Gen + high-garbage Old Gen regions
   - Multiple rounds, each with a short pause
   - This is G1's secret: targeted, incremental Old Gen collection

4. Full GC (emergency, last resort):
   - Single-threaded by default until Java 10 (then parallel)
   - Long pause (seconds)
   - Triggered when G1 can't keep up with allocation
   - Target: never happen in production
```

## Production Reality

The most impactful GC tuning for Spring Boot services: set `-Xms` = `-Xmx` (prevents dynamic heap resizing), tune `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis` for G1GC based on your SLA (200ms is reasonable for APIs), and always enable GC logging. Don't tune blindly — GC log analysis with a tool (GCEasy.io, GCViewer) will show you what's actually happening. The most common GC problem in Spring Boot apps is unbounded caches filling Old Gen — switch from HashMap caches to Caffeine with a size limit.
